A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, methods, principal theorems, and retained examples. The full text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: Section 7 and Table 1 report original SOS-versus-PGD experiments on randomly generated games. Appendix H reports computed optimal strategies, objective values, and runtimes.

after.justification: Section 7 reports original comparison and scalability experiments in Tables 1–2. Appendix I retains computed examples and adds results on 100 generalized absentminded-driver instances.

M1.justification: Section 3 corrects the polynomial KKT multiplier signs, and Appendix G corrects the corresponding Select/Verify stationarity constraints. These locally revise the stated KKT formulation; the Moment-SOS hierarchy, vertex restriction, SVC steps, and extraction procedure remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix I adds a structured generalized absentminded-driver benchmark involving successive repeated information sets and continuation/termination actions. This supplements the retained random polynomial games and individual examples. Increasing dimensions and degrees within the existing random-game family changes settings rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: PGD remains the sole evaluated comparison method in Table 1. The newly cited work on local optimization motivates this baseline but is not separately evaluated; the scalability and driver experiments report SOS alone.

E3.justification: The reported SOS order is revised across experiments: v1 states d equals the utility degree, whereas v2 specifies truncation degree DSOS = 2d equal to the utility degree. The quartic appendix example explicitly changes from d = 4 to d = 2. These are revised reported settings, without establishing reruns. V2 also adds a sweep reaching nine information sets and degree 16, plus a specified 100-instance driver protocol.

E4.justification: Section 7.2 and Table 2 extend the existing runtime sensitivity analysis to larger combinations of information-set counts and polynomial degrees, documenting prohibitively expensive regions. The question remains computational scaling; the original theorem-illustrating appendix examples are retained, without new component ablations or robustness tests.

E5.justification: The retained comparison still averages 50 random instances with 100 PGD restarts per instance. Neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new driver experiment adds sampled game instances, not a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 updates runtimes and some success rates: for two information sets and degree 10, SOS time changes from 9.04 to 6.64 seconds and PGD success from 85.56% to 87.14%. It also adds a six-information-set row. New Table 2 substantially expands runtime results, and Appendix I reports driver success on 100/100 instances with mean runtime 1.56 seconds. Revised order reporting prevents treating the timing updates as established same-setting speedups.

T1.justification: Section 3 and new Appendix D replace the measure-zero description of genericity with an algebraic exceptional-set formulation, including active-set discriminants and a worked determinant example. V2 also corrects KKT signs, realization-probability product limits, and the certificate order in the proof of Theorem 6.3. The principal theorem statements and proof structures remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: asymptotic convergence, generic finite convergence, information-set-dependent exactness for single-player non-absentminded games, and first-level exactness for SOS-concave/monotone single-player games. The added experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains genericity relative to fixed game structures and admissible utility classes, including zero-sum constraints. It interprets SOS as runtime-competitive on smaller instances while making scalability limits more concrete. Appendix I also relabels the retained quartic from SOS-convex to SOS-concave without changing its polynomial, leaving its claimed corroboration of Theorem 6.3 inconsistent.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses eliminating one redundant variable per information set before constructing the SDP. It adds repository/script access information, a supplementary-code statement, and the driver benchmark's generation recipe. Julia, SumOfSquares, processor, RAM, and operating-system disclosures were already present in v1.

R1.justification: V2 adds Fearnley et al. and Tewolde et al. to position PGD and distinguish local optimization from certified global solutions. Harris and Lazard–Rouillier support the genericity discussion. The broader related-work positioning, including the tree-decomposition comparison, is retained.

P1.justification: Section 7 is renamed and reorganized into comparison and scalability subsections. V2 adds a genericity appendix and acknowledgement, impact, and reproducibility statements, alongside terminology and copyediting corrections. Most existing prose and the overall scientific narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, with resized and repositioned figures and reformatted equations. Table 1 drops the variable-count column and revises degree labels and its caption; a new runtime-grid Table 2 is added. The original complexity table is retained as Table 3.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs consequential KKT and mathematical inconsistencies, clarifies experimental orders and implementation, and adds useful evidence about scalability and a structured benchmark. Code-access information also improves reproducibility. These benefits support a net improvement, although the unchanged quartic newly labeled SOS-concave still fails to support its claimed theoretical illustration.
